nameStory: This microscopic green alga gets its name from the Greek word 'aster' meaning star, combined with 'coccus' meaning berry or sphere. The 'superbus' part means 'superb' or 'magnificent' in Latin, which seems like quite a grand name for something you need a microscope to see properly!
description: Asterococcus superbus is a tiny single-celled green alga that forms small, jelly-like colonies on tree bark and rocks. Each colony looks like a small green blob or cushion, usually no bigger than a few millimeters across. Under a magnifying glass, you might see the individual star-shaped cells that give this species its name. It's part of the vast world of microorganisms that quietly live all around us in New England forests.

idTips.label: Colony appearance
idTips.description: Small green, jelly-like blobs on bark that feel slightly squishy and damp to the touch, like tiny green gumdrops

idTips.label: Location on trees
idTips.description: Found in crevices and rough spots on tree bark, especially where moisture collects after rain

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to olive green when wet, becoming darker and more brownish when dried out

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies are typically 1-5 millimeters across, about the size of a small peppercorn or smaller

idTips.label: Texture when wet
idTips.description: Gelatinous and slightly slippery, like touching a small piece of wet seaweed or algae

habitat: Look for this tiny alga on the bark of deciduous trees in moist woodlands throughout New England, especially in areas with high humidity. It prefers the north-facing sides of trees and spots where water naturally collects, such as bark crevices near streams or in shaded forest understories. You'll have the best luck finding it in areas that stay damp for extended periods.

seasonality.spring: Colonies become more visible and vibrant green as spring moisture returns, swelling up after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid summer months, especially after rain when colonies are plump and bright green.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but may begin to shrink and darken as temperatures cool and humidity drops.
seasonality.winter: Colonies appear shrunken and dark, entering a dormant state but still present on bark surfaces.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye individually, these tiny algae can actually help clean our air by absorbing carbon dioxide and producing oxygen right on tree bark - essentially turning every tree trunk into a mini air purifier!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small green algae or even tiny mosses growing on bark. The key difference is the jelly-like, squishy texture that distinguishes algae from the more structured, leafy appearance of mosses.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of those organisms that reminds us how much life exists at scales we rarely notice. While we admire the big trees in New England forests, countless microscopic communities like this one are quietly thriving on every surface around us.
compareHints: **Note: Limited information available for this rare species - only 3 documented observations in New England.** Since this is the only Asterococcus species in our regional dataset, compare it with other bark-dwelling green algae in the same family, which typically have similar jelly-like colonies but may lack the distinctive star-shaped cell structure. Most related species form similar small, gelatinous green patches but have different cellular arrangements visible under magnification.
